title: Generating Real-World Evidence From AI Deployed in Health Systems

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Generating Real-World Evidence From AI Deployed in Health Systems》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · lrh270131-sec-0005-p1】Learning health systems increasingly deploy artificial intelligence (AI) within routine care delivery. Because these tools are digitally embedded in clinical workflows, their use generates clinical, operational, and interaction data that can support evaluation. In this Brief Report, we use real‐world evidence (RWE) to refer to evidence generated by analyzing data arising from the routine deployment and use of AI‐enabled workflows. We focus on research questions concerning the safety and effectiveness of these workflows and local quality‐improvement decisions about refinement. Regulatory, accountability, and high‐stakes reliability claims may require additional standardized measurement, independent adjudication, or purpose‐designed data collection beyond the scope of this framework [1, 2].

【Introduction · lrh270131-sec-0005-p2】Persistent resource constraints motivate the use of AI in health care. Clinical demand exceeds available capacity, requiring continual reallocation of human effort across patient populations and tasks [1, 2, 3, 4]. AI is incorporated into care delivery workflows in two broad forms: predictive and generative AI. Predictive AI uses clinical and operational data to estimate the risk of future events, with interventions prioritized for high‐risk patients. Generative AI extracts, summarizes, and communicates information and can be connected to external knowledge sources and software tools to support multistep or agentic workflows. Such workflows may automate selected tasks while escalating cases that meet predefined criteria for clinical review [3, 4]. The need for automation is underscored by a recent Utah program allowing AI models to refill prescription medications [5] and the nascent ARPA‐H Agentic AI‐EnableD CardioVascular CAre TransfOrmation (ADVOCATE) program [6]. Across these forms of implementation, a central question is how learning health systems should generate rigorous RWE on AI‐enabled workflows with different forms of human oversight and automation.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Generating Real-World Evidence From AI Deployed in Health Systems》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Human‐in‐the‐Loop Implementation · lrh270131-sec-0013-p2】Determining whether an AI‐enabled workflow is effective requires causal evaluation, ideally through randomization when feasible and, in routine deployment, often through quasi‐experimental causal inference designs. HITL workflows can induce feedback loops, in which the intervention triggered by the AI model alters observed model performance [12, 17]. Changes in observed performance may therefore reflect the intervention rather than algorithmic drift. Algorithmic drift refers broadly to changes in model performance over time as the underlying data or relationships between predictors and outcomes change and is an important target of post‐deployment monitoring [17, 18]. For example, if an AI‐triggered intervention prevents adverse outcomes among patients identified as high risk, the observed association between predictions and outcomes may weaken even when the workflow is beneficial [12, 17]. Observed changes may therefore reflect intervention effects, workflow adaptation, changes in case mix, or algorithmic drift [17, 18]. Monitoring and RWE generation overlap in both the data they use and the questions they address, particularly in HOTL and automated implementations. Routine monitoring data may contribute to RWE when analyzed to address a defined clinical, operational, or implementation question using methods appropriate to the intended inference.

【Human‐on‐the‐Loop Implementation · lrh270131-sec-0014-p1】When predictive AI is used in a HOTL approach, the model drives an action that is subsequently (i.e., asynchronously) reviewed by a human. Certain models, such as conformal prediction models, may produce an “I don't know” when the training data are not sufficiently representative for a given prediction [23]. Compared with HITL, evaluation of HOTL predictive AI places greater emphasis on whether cases are appropriately escalated for human review and whether errors remain detectable and correctable when identified during asynchronous oversight.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Generating Real-World Evidence From AI Deployed in Health Systems》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusion · lrh270131-sec-0021-p1】Learning health systems need RWE strategies that match how AI is implemented and overseen. Silent deployment is important for establishing local validity and identifying subgroup differences, but it cannot determine whether AI‐enabled workflows improve outcomes once predictions or generated content drive action. Once AI outputs influence care, generating credible RWE requires study designs that support causal inference, together with evaluation of escalation pathways and measurement of human workload, including residual follow‐up work. Organizing RWE generation by implementation configuration supports rapid learning cycles and informs whether an AI‐enabled workflow should be continued, refined, scaled, automated, or decommissioned.

【Results · abstract-3-1】Each implementation configuration supports different forms of evidence about model performance, workflow effectiveness, human oversight, and safety. For both predictive and generative AI, silent deployment supports assessment of local performance and subgroup differences. Once predictive AI drives action, evaluating the effectiveness of an implemented workflow (HITL, HOTL, or automated) generally requires causal inference approaches. For generative AI, HITL implementations can generate data on edits, overrides, time on task, usability, cognitive burden, and safety-relevant failure modes. HOTL and automated generative AI implementations can generate data on escalation performance, human follow-up work, downstream outcomes, and safety signals.

sections.text:

【AI Implementation Configurations · lrh270131-sec-0006-p1】We use the following operational definitions, which distinguish configurations according to how model outputs affect clinical workflows and how human oversight is structured.

【Human‐in‐the‐Loop Implementation · lrh270131-sec-0013-p1】When predictive models trigger outreach, triage, alerts, or other actions, they become part of an intervention. In this configuration, the key question is whether the AI‐enabled workflow improves outcomes. Having a HITL means that risk scores produced by the model are reviewed by a human before being acted upon. High concordance between risk estimates and user actions may reflect appropriate reliance, but it may also reflect overreliance.
